cub.e: From earlier cubbe. Origin unknown. According to Pokorny, from Proto-Germanic *kubb-, from Proto-Indo-European *gup- (“round object, knoll”), from *gew- (“to bend, curve, convex, arch, vault”). Related terms include cup (cf. cupboard), coffin, cove, etc, essentially “chamber”, thus cub maybe initially derived from the sense “den”, or maybe “womb”.
cub.g: The young of certain animals, chiefly large carnivorous mammals, including the bear, wolf, fox, lion and tiger.

cubit.e: From Middle English cubite, from Latin cubitum (“elbow, cubit”).
cubit.g: The distance from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger used as an informal unit of length.

cucumber.e: From Middle English cucumer, cucumber, from Old French cocombre, ultimately from Latin cucumis, cucumerem (possibly through an Old Occitan intermediate). Probably of Pre-Italic substrate origin.
cucumber.g: A vine in the gourd family, Cucumis sativus.

cud.e: From Middle English code, cudde, coude, quede, quide, from Old English cudu, cwidu, from Proto-West Germanic *kwidu, from Proto-Germanic *kweduz (“resin”).
cud.g: The portion of food which is brought back into the mouth by ruminants from their rumen, to be chewed a second time.

cultivate.e: From Medieval Latin cultivātus, perfect passive participle of cultivō (“till, cultivate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) for more), from cultīvus (“tilled”), from Latin cultus, perfect passive participle of colō (“till, cultivate”), which comes from earlier *quelō, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷel- (“to move; to turn (around)”).

cumber.e: From Middle English combren, aphetic form of acombren or encombren, borrowed from Old French encombrer, ultimately either from Latin cumulus or Proto-Celtic *kombereti (“to bring together”), from *kom- + *bereti (“to bear”).
cumber.g: To slow down; to hinder; to burden; to encumber.

cumber.e: From Middle English komber, kumbre, cumbre, combre (“distress; destruction”). Used in 14th century Middle English in the very scarcely attested “destruction” sense but not in common use until the 16th century; at first chiefly Scots, where it is also spelled cummer.

cumin.e: From Middle English comyn, from Old English cymen (which is cognate with Old High German kumin) and Old French cummin, both from Latin cuminum, from Ancient Greek κύμινον (kúminon), a Semitic borrowing ultimately to be traced to Akkadian 𒂵𒈬𒉡 (Ú.GAMUN /⁠kamūnu⁠/, “cumin”). Possibly related to caraway.
cumin.g: The flowering plant Cuminum cyminum, in the family Apiaceae.

cunning.e: From Middle English cunning, kunning, konnyng, alteration of earlier Middle English cunninde, kunnende, cunnand, from Old English cunnende, present participle of cunnan (“to know how to, be able to”), equivalent to con + -ing.
cunning.g: Sly; crafty; clever in surreptitious behaviour.

cunning.e: From Middle English cunning, kunnyng, partially from Old English *cunning (verbal noun), from Old English cunnan (“to know how to, be able to”); partially from Old English cunnung (“knowledge, trial, probation, experience, contact, carnal knowledge”).
cunning.g: Practical knowledge or experience; aptitude in performance; skill, proficiency; dexterity.

cup.e: From Middle English cuppe, coppe, from the merger of Old English cuppe (“cup”) and Old English copp (“cup, vessel”). Old English cuppe is a borrowing from Late Latin cuppa, itself of obscure origin, but probably from earlier Latin cūpa (“tub, cask”), from Proto-Indo-European *kewp- (“a hollow”).
cup.g: A concave vessel for drinking, usually made of opaque material (as opposed to a glass) and with a handle.

cupbearer.g: One who ceremonially fills and hands out the cups in which a drink is served.

curd.e: From Middle English curd, a metathetic variant of crud, crudde (“coagulated substance”).
curd.g: The coagulated part of any liquid.

curdle.e: Metathesis of earlier dialectal cruddle, crudle, equivalent to curd + -le (frequentative suffix).
curdle.g: To form curds so that it no longer flows smoothly; to cause to form such curds. (usually said of milk)

cure.e: From Middle English cure, borrowed from Old French cure (“care, cure, healing, cure of souls”), from Latin cura (“care, medical attendance, cure”).
cure.g: A method, device or medication that restores good health.

cure.e: From Middle English curen, from Old French curer, from Latin cūrāre. Partially displaced Old English ġehǣlan, whence Modern English heal.

curious.e: From Middle English curious, from Old French curius, from Latin cūriōsus. The English word is cognate with Italian curioso, Occitan curios, Portuguese curioso, and Spanish curioso.
curious.g: Tending to ask questions, or to want to explore or investigate; inquisitive; (with a negative connotation) nosy, prying.

curiously.e: From Middle English curiusly, curyously, curiosly, curiouseliche, curyouslyche, equivalent to curious + -ly.
curiously.g: In a curious manner; with curiosity; inquisitively.

curl.e: From metathesis of Middle English crulle (“curled, curly”), of uncertain origin but probably from an unrecorded Old English word or from Middle Dutch crul, crulle (“curl”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *kruzlǭ (“bent or crooked object, curl”), connected to *krūsą (“curl”), of unknown origin.
curl.g: A curving piece or lock of hair; a ringlet.

current.e: From Middle English curraunt, borrowed from Old French curant (French courant), present participle of courre (“to run”), from Latin currere (“to run”) (present participle currens).
current.g: The generally unidirectional movement of a gas or fluid.

curse.e: From Middle English curse, kors, cors, curs, from Old English cors, curs (“curse”), of unknown origin.
curse.g: A supernatural detriment or hindrance; a bane.

curse.e: From Middle English cursen, corsen, coursen, from Old English corsian, cursian (“to curse”), from the noun (see above).
curse.g: To place a curse upon (a person or object).

cursed.e: From Middle English cursed, cursd, curst, corsed, curset, cursyd, equivalent to curse + -ed.
cursed.g: Under some divine harm, malady, or other curse.

cursing.e: From Middle English kursyng, from Old English cursiende, equivalent to curse + -ing.

curtain.e: From Middle English curtine, from Old French cortine, from Late Latin cōrtīna (“curtain”), a calque from Ancient Greek.
curtain.g: A piece of cloth covering a window, bed, etc. to offer privacy and keep out light.

cushion.e: From Middle English quysshyn, from later Old French coissin (modern coussin), from Vulgar Latin *coxīnus (“seat pad”), derived from Latin coxa (“hip, thigh”) (with the suffix possibly after Latin pulvīnus (“pillow”)), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *koḱs- (“joint, limb”).
cushion.g: A soft mass of material stuffed into a cloth bag, used for comfort or support.

custodian.e: From a shortening of Latin custōdiānātus, from Latin custōdia (“a keeping, watch, guard, prison”), from custōs (“a keeper, watchman, guard”). By surface analysis, custody + -ian.
custodian.g: A person entrusted with the custody or care of something or someone; a caretaker or keeper.

custody.e: Borrowed from Latin custōdia (“a keeping, watch, guard, prison”), from custōs (“a keeper, watchman, guard”).
custody.g: The legal right to take care of something or somebody, especially children.

custom.e: From Middle English custume, borrowed from Anglo-Norman custume, inherited from Latin consuētūdinem, a noun derived from cōnsuēscō, from con- (“with”) + suēscō (“become used or accustomed to”). The adjectival form first appears c. 1830.
custom.g: Frequent repetition of the same behavior; way of behavior common to many; ordinary manner; habitual practice; method of doing, living or beh

customary.e: From Middle English custumary, from Medieval Latin custumarius. By surface analysis, custom + -ary.
customary.g: In accordance with, or established by, custom or common usage.

customer.e: From Middle English custumer, from Old French coustumier, costumier (compare modern French coutumier), from Medieval Latin custumarius (“a toll-gatherer, tax-collector”, noun), from custumarius (“pertaining to custom or customs”, adjective), from custuma (“custom, tax”). By surface analysis, custom + -er.
customer.g: A habitual patron, regular purchaser, returning client; a person or company who has a custom of buying from a particular business.

customs.e: Plural of custom. Perhaps influenced by or taken as a corruption of customhouse, from Middle English custome hous.
customs.g: The duties or taxes imposed on imported or exported goods.

cut.e: From Middle English cutten, of North Germanic origin, from Old Norse *kytja, *kutta, from Proto-Germanic *kutjaną, *kuttaną (“to cut”), of uncertain origin, perhaps related to Proto-Germanic *kwetwą (“meat, flesh”) (compare Old Norse kvett (“meat”)). Sometimes instead compared to French couteau, itself from Latin culter (“knife”).
cut.g: To incise, to cut into the surface of something.

cutter.e: From Middle English cutter, cuttere, kutter. By surface analysis, cut + -er.
cutter.g: A person or device that cuts (in various senses).

cutting.g: The action of the verb to cut.
